This quarter (my first quarter at UCSD as a transfer student) was the first time I ever used AI to help with my coursework. It was suggested by my math professor and she gave us guidelines on how to use it. If I am having trouble knowing where to start on a problem (sometimes a complex word problem where I'm not sure what equation to use, sometimes a complex rational equation where I don't know which step should come first depending on if we're simplifying, adding, subtracting, etc.) and cannot figure it out using our textbook or notes, she has permitted us to put the problem into a generative AI domain and ask it to help us with the first step to the problem. Another way I use it (suggested by same math professor) is to ask it to give me a bunch of practice questions of a section I am struggling on. So for example, yesterday while studying for our midterm on Friday, I asked it to give me 10 practice questions on finding the leading terms of quadratic expressions. I did these problems, gave my answers, and then it (Gemini) corrected my mistakes and guided me to through the corrections. I don't use it with any other subject, especially not my major/intended career subjects, because I feel that it offloads my thinking and I actually like my brain and would like to keep it that way.

On Reddit earlier today I was looking up stuff related to the Learjet crash in Florida and when I opened the app, since I follow UCSD, the first suggested post was someone talking about how one of their bio profs were using AI to generate the lecture slides and then trying to make it make sense in real time while teaching. As if he hadn't seen the material. Students in the comments seemed to know who this prof was even if he had taught different courses and said that he generally was a really nice person and prof and that he was really knowledgable about the subject, but wasn't able to put it together enough to make slides independent from AI. They said that he would give great breakdowns of the material in his office hours but in class it seemed like there was too much material on the slide but it didn't actually mean anything, and that he wouldn't be able to answer for errors on the lecture slides. The comments suggested that they go to a school journal/newspaper or go straight to the department for a complaint, and some told them to ask the prof or TA directly. Personally, I'm not sure how I would handle that situation but seems like that's a tough one. Now I don't know if the prof is an associate professor or a full professor with a PhD/MD as they didn't mention his name and I didn't bother looking through all of the bio profs, but if he is a full prof with a research or medical degree, he should be able to at least put something together if he is going to teach at this school. People are paying a lot of money to get a degree here that means something to the world, and then are being met with potentially AI-generated stuff in the classrooms, and I 100% understand their frustration because I would hate that too.

In some areas like computer science, the degree is basically becoming an AI assistant degree, from what I hear from my CS friends. So many people are turning away from CS because of that and I feel like at some point there will either be a serious lack of oversight of these AI bots and companies because no one really understands how it's all working. If we don't know how something works, how are we supposed to have it under control? Government oversight is another really big concern of mine. National security (recent example Jensen Huang at Nvidia and concerns about intelligence and spying), personal data collection malpractice, data centers, global warming, animal displacement, community interference, etc.. And it's all just being shoved into our faces. The FAA grounded all domestic flights last week for the first time since 9/11, probably because of a failed AI integration at the hands of the US government, and that should be highly disconcerting to anyone who hears about it. On the other hand, there are some really great implementations of genAI in the real world. Disability assistance, and medical assistance, especially with diagnostics, are two that come to mind. But again, there needs to be some sort of centralized or formal control over these very powerful tools. As with everything powerful, it can go either way and end up in the wrong hands, and there are tradeoffs.
